_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Science unit lecture film, Lesson 4 Growing Up. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON['lecture'] in order (the frog; the butterfly; babies and chicks; two ways to grow up; two kinds of model), with the lesson's own record step between the last two, and they use the lesson's own pictures: the kit's frogspawn, tadpole, tadpole with legs, froglet, chrysalis and ladybird larva drawings, and the emoji its steps give each animal.
title: Growing Up
subtitle: Grade 3 Science
objectives: Describe and compare how the offspring of different animals grow into adults, including humans, birds, frogs and butterflies.
Know that there are different types of models in science, including diagrams and physical models that we can touch.
Use observations and tests to sort, group and classify objects.
Collect and record observations and/or measurements in tables and diagrams.

beats.say: Every animal starts small and grows up. Some change shape on the way.
A tadpole becomes a frog. A caterpillar becomes a butterfly.
A frog starts as eggs in jelly in a pond. This is frogspawn.
A tadpole hatches. It has a tail and no legs, and breathes in the water.
Back legs grow first, then front legs. The tail starts to shrink.
Now it is a froglet: legs front and back, and a stub of tail. It can climb out.
An adult frog has no tail and breathes air. It lays eggs of its own.
A tadpole is not a baby fish. It is a baby frog that does not look like one.
A butterfly starts as a tiny egg, laid on a leaf.
A caterpillar hatches and eats leaves all day, growing and growing.
Then it hangs itself up and becomes a chrysalis. It stays very still.
Inside the chrysalis it is changing completely. It has not died.
A butterfly comes out, dries its wings, and flies off to lay eggs.
A human baby cannot walk or talk yet, and it drinks milk.
But it already has the shape of a person. It only grows bigger.
A child, then an adult, fully grown. That takes many years.
A chick hatches fluffy. In a few weeks it has feathers and can fly.
Same shape, bigger. A bird does not change shape like a frog.
So there are two ways to grow up. Sort each baby animal.
Keep your shape and get bigger: a puppy, a chick, a foal, a kitten, a baby.
Or change shape completely: a tadpole, a caterpillar, a ladybird larva.
Do not go by size. Look for the change of shape.
Animals take different times to grow up. A table lets you compare them.
A butterfly: egg to butterfly in only a few weeks.
A frog: frogspawn to froglet takes a few months.
A human takes many years. The bigger the animal, the longer it takes.
Scientists use models. A model shows an idea clearly, leaving the rest out.
A drawing of the frog's life cycle, with labels, is a diagram. You read it.
A plastic butterfly with wings that open is a physical model.
A globe, or a toy skeleton. You can hold a physical model and turn it.
A frog and a butterfly change shape completely as they grow.
A chick and a baby keep their shape and only get bigger.
Every animal grows up at its own speed: weeks, months or years.
A diagram you read. A physical model you hold. Both show an idea.
